Action Relationships

How a name pair is made

Label Studio connects each English action name to annotated spans in the source films. Each unique name has one stored vector.

When similar names describe different assembly conditions

“Hold timber at joint” and “Position timber at joint” score 0.897. Their recorded axes change in opposite directions.

Compare the two recorded events ↗

Assembly Space

Atlas of Assembly Space ↗ Compare two cases ↗

From video to top view

V22 S01 follows surface features through the film to produce a local top view and a schematic overlay on the workshop plan.

A tool approaches a joint, a grip shifts, and a piece of timber is guided into place. We align three moments from the footage to see how adjustments like these unfold.

Select a highlighted interval on a case timeline to open its board.

Music in both films: Getting it Done by Kevin MacLeod (CC BY 4.0), excerpt with fades.

How action pairs are selected

The wheel shows all qualifying name pairs with drawings on both sides. “No shared case” keeps names whose case sets do not overlap. “Connected group at 0.65” orders actions by graph component.

Precomputed cosine scores measure similarity between action names. Use the drawings to compare the physical operations, geometry and direction.

V29

V29

Kyjánek, Al Bahar, Vasey, Wannemacher, and Menges, “Implementation of an Augmented Reality AR Workflow for Human Robot Collaboration in Timber Prefabrication,” ISARC, 2019. doi:10.22260/ISARC2019/0164

Human–robot

V29 · Three roles in the same moment

The record describes a gripper holding the member, a hand steadying it, and a person operating a power tool during the same interval.

Open question: how is support transferred when one of these roles releases the member?

How to read V29. At 88.0–90.3 s the gripper holds, a hand steadies, and a person uses a power tool on the same frames. Thirteen human tracks have zero saved duration; the frame evidence still shows participation.
